transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump is praising Stephen Miller ahead of his move to White House Chief of Staff on Monday.
Miller replaces Suzy Wiles following Republicans' losses in the midterm elections.
Trump spoke last night at an event honoring astronauts at Cape Canaveral.
He's very loyal, smart. He does a great job. He's been an MVP every year.
Miller currently serves as Deputy Chief of Staff and has worked with Trump since the 2016 presidential campaign.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could face a House impeachment vote as soon as next week.
Kentucky Republican Tom Massey plans to revive the effort when lawmakers return on Monday.
Massey accuses Hegseth of waging war against Iran without congressional approval.
The push follows Republican midterm losses that party leaders have linked to the war.
Hegseth has vowed to fight impeachment, and President Trump continues to support him.
The backlash against the president's immigration enforcement tactics played a role in this week's Republican losses, especially in Texas.
NPR's Sergio Martinez-Beltran reports Democrats are weighing a seismic political shift that many see as a mandate on immigration policy.
Exit polling shows immigration was top of mind for voters.
In Texas, two men have been killed by ICE agents, including Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, who was shot to death on his way to work.
His son, Ronaldo Salgado, says the results should make the new Democratic majority reflect.
Unfortunately, Texas has become the epicenter of ICE enforcement and gross violence against immigrants, and the voters spoken.
The incoming lawmakers have a duty to listen to us.
Locally, immigrant rights advocates say they want the state to stop collaborating with ICE.
Nationally, they want less funding for ICE and oversight.
Sergio Martinez-Beltran, NPR News, Austin, Texas.
Google, Meta, and TikTok are suing California to block a new law aimed at shielding kids from addictive social media features.
Rachel Miro of member station KQED reports.
In separate lawsuits, Google, Meta, and TikTok argue the new law, which takes effect in January, violates their free speech rights and wrongly substitutes the state's judgment for that of parents.
Rin Alajaji is with the digital rights group, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which opposed the bill.
It's a functional ban for young people under 16.
It cuts young people off from essential information and experiences online.
It silences the very voices it plans to protect.
The California Attorney General's office says it's reviewing the lawsuits, adding, quote,
"our office is committed to defending California's common sense laws to protect kids online."
For NPR News, I'm Rachel Miro.
This is NPR.
More protests are expected across France today, two days after a nationwide strike attracted more than a half million people.
As Rebecca Rossman reports, the demonstration started over a month ago as a student movement, but has evolved into a national push for better living conditions.
France's Interior Minister says 70,000 police officers will be mobilized for today's protests.
What started as a student movement calling for better conditions in schools has evolved into a national push to address wider inequalities across French society.
Today's protests come just two days after a nationwide strike drew in more than half a million people,
including an impromptu orchestra that assembled at the Place de la République in Paris.
Just last month, demonstrations in the same neighborhood turned violent when dozens of businesses were looted, costing millions in damages.
The prime minister is scheduled to meet with union heads and businesses on Monday to come up with solutions.
Rebecca Rossman and peer news, Paris.
The Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi remain undecided as ballot counting continues.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola holds a narrow lead over Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, with more results expected Monday and Tuesday.
In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by roughly 2,600 votes, with thousands of ballots still outstanding.
The outcomes will determine how much Democrats expand the Senate majority they've already secured.
This is NPR News.

Trump speaks at Cape Canaveral event honoring astronauts
Kentucky Republican Tom Massey plans to revive impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
Texas immigration enforcement backlash shapes Republican midterm losses, with Houston ICE shooting cited
Google, Meta, and TikTok sue California to block law restricting addictive social media features for kids
France braces for more protests after nationwide strike drew over half a million people
Alaska and Mississippi Senate races remain undecided as ballot counting continues
